title: Encounters with the Other
author: Barry Oshry
status: Abridged animated adaptation with synthetic narration, for Barry Oshry's review.

scenes.title:
Encounters with
the Other
scenes.text:
An animated adaptation of Barry Oshry's book.
For the peacemakers.

scenes.title:
How could people
do this?
scenes.text: A child learns of the Holocaust. Fear becomes anger. The question stays with him as he grows up and learns of other horrors.

scenes.title: The question changes
scenes.text:
The words remain. The tone changes.
How does hatred begin?
When, and from whom, do we learn it?

scenes.chapter: Act I · How cultures come to be
scenes.title: Our ordinary world
scenes.text:
Another culture may look strange to us.
Our culture may look strange to them.
Neither feels strange from the inside.

scenes.chapter: Act I · How cultures come to be
scenes.title: We learn the rules
scenes.text: Parents, elders, teachers, peers, and media teach us how to speak, dress, grieve, celebrate, seek justice, and live with one another.

scenes.chapter: Act I · How cultures come to be
scenes.title:
The rules become
invisible
scenes.text: We learn them so well that we stop experiencing them as rules. They become the lens through which we see the world.

scenes.chapter: Act I · How cultures come to be
scenes.title: And then we meet
scenes.text: Each culture experiences its own ways as how things are, or ought to be. Neither experiences them simply as one possibility among many.

scenes.title:
Difference becomes
a threat
scenes.text: The 'other' arrives, is conquered, or becomes visible. Through our lens, unfamiliar behaviour can look wrong, upsetting, or dangerous to our way of life.

scenes.title: Loose and tight
scenes.text: We may reflexively allow the unfamiliar, or reflexively reject it. Both responses can spare us the discomfort of engaging with its complexity.

scenes.title: Moral positions
scenes.text: Oshry distinguishes these reflexes from liberal and conservative responses grounded in values: including the other, or preserving and protecting the existing culture.

scenes.title: Conviction and conflict
scenes.text: Some hold either position firmly. Many of us are conflicted: welcoming at one moment, rejecting at another. These responses can occur within the same person.

scenes.title: The tolerance solution
scenes.text: The other is allowed to coexist, with restrictions and recurring tension. Acceptance and rejection pull against one another. Such arrangements can endure for generations.

scenes.title: The purity solution
scenes.text: Rejection overwhelms acceptance. The other is cast as a pollutant or threat. Confinement, suppression, exile, or destruction becomes a means of preserving the culture.

scenes.title: Tolerance can collapse
scenes.text: An arrangement that appears settled may turn into catastrophe. In Oshry's account, both solutions also diminish the oppressor, whose worth depends on the other's diminished worth.

scenes.title: Become like us?
scenes.text: Assimilation can bring acceptance. Some cannot become indistinguishable; some have no wish to. And acceptance can prove conditional when resources shrink, threats grow, and demagogues intervene.

scenes.title:
An assumption
inside assimilation
scenes.text:
It takes the host culture to be the best destination.
Why would everyone want to become just like us?

scenes.title: Substitute knowledge
scenes.text: We believe we know the other. In the absence of real encounter, fears, desires, projections, and a demagogue's stories can fill the gap.

scenes.title:
Certainty without
knowing
scenes.text: Those stories justify our feelings and actions. Like-minded groups repeat them. Separation grows, while our picture of the other seems increasingly certain.

scenes.title: What about laws?
scenes.text: Laws can offer protection and a route to justice. Oshry argues that they cannot, by themselves, make us see the other differently. What could change our seeing?

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Power seeing
scenes.text:
In this book, power means seeing
difference and separateness.
The other is different from us and unconnected to us.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Love seeing
scenes.text:
Love means seeing
commonality and connectedness.
The other is like us and connected to us.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: A fuller experience
scenes.text: We can experience both: our differences and our common humanity; our separate lives and our connections. Oshry calls this robust seeing.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: The power reflex
scenes.text: Unfamiliar behaviour can draw our attention towards difference and separateness. Without awareness or choice, these may become the whole of our experience.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: A reinforcing cycle
scenes.text: Staying separate strengthens our experience of difference. Experiencing difference encourages us to stay separate. Each reinforces the other.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Power without love
scenes.text: Commonality and connectedness recede. We become capable of doing to the other what we would never do to those we experience as our own.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: 'Not with these people'
scenes.text: From inside the pattern, connection can seem foolish or dangerous. Our picture of the other feels solid. We mistake the effects of the relationship for who they really are.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: System sight
scenes.text: The patterns we fall into shape how we experience ourselves and others. Seeing the pattern opens another possibility: changing how we relate.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Change the pattern
scenes.text: Counterbalance separateness with connection. Build ongoing relationships through work that matters to everyone involved.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title:
Something to do
together
scenes.text: Build housing. Share meals. Cultivate land. Write and produce a play. Work on a community project. The connection is ongoing and mutually meaningful.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: The love cycle
scenes.text: Working together can reveal commonality. Experiencing commonality supports further connection. This, too, is a reinforcing cycle.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Difference remains
scenes.text: Connection also lets us encounter differences more directly, with less room for myths, fantasies, fears, and projections. Love supports a fuller experience of power as well as love.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: Power and love
scenes.text:
Same and different.
Separate and connected.
Free to pursue our separate ways and to join in work that matters to us together.

scenes.chapter: Act III · Seeing through power and love
scenes.title: A possibility to test
scenes.text: Oshry asks us to test whether changing the pattern changes our experience. From inside system blindness, the possibility may still seem inconceivable.

scenes.title: The sacred mission
scenes.text: Oppression can be justified as revenge, defence of sacred territory, protection of belief, or the creation of a perfect society. The other becomes an obstacle to the mission.

scenes.title: The demagogue's offer
scenes.text: Our purity. Our superiority. Their inferiority. A promise to protect the culture by dominating or eliminating the other, and those who support them.

scenes.title: Protective stories
scenes.text: A culture may deny a catastrophe, or describe its own violence as necessary self-defence. Its image of innocence survives at the expense of those who suffered.

scenes.title: A record of suffering
scenes.text: The book recalls Armenia, the Holocaust, the Partition of India, Cambodia, Rwanda, Srebrenica, and many other catastrophes. Its catalogue asks us to recognise a recurring human possibility.

scenes.title: Enough
scenes.text: Oshry notes that his historical summary is incomplete and disputed. This adaptation condenses it without reproducing its casualty estimates or presenting its dated accounts as current reporting.

scenes.title: A third possibility
scenes.text: Beyond the book's tolerance and purity solutions lies another relationship: power and love together. Changing the pattern can change how we experience one another.

scenes.title: Teach the children
scenes.text: Oshry returns to the child's question. He imagines children learning how oppression begins and how it can end, through stories, songs, drama, and the histories of their own cultures.

scenes.title: Recognise the invitation
scenes.text: His afterword warns of leaders and media interests that prosper by offering us an other to fear. Awareness gives us a choice about whether to join them.

scenes.title:
'I am here to
teach the children'
scenes.text:
The closing commitment in Barry Oshry's afterword.
What relationship could you change?
What might become possible?
